extractions.quote: The most striking clinical feature of our patient was the presence of painful spasms of the right thigh which occurred spontaneously or were induced by voluntary action or unexpected noises. These spasms were also associated with stiffness of the neck muscles. Limb dystonia is unlikely, because dystonic spasms are generally less painful and not stimulus-sensitive. Spasticity can be excluded, because there were no upper motor neuron signs and central motor conduction time was normal. The association of stimulus-sensitive spasms and CMUA in leg muscles is seen in several diseases involving the spinal cord. Its long tract involvement, abnormal cerebrospinal fluid, and catastrophic course can easily differentiate idiopathic encephalomyelitis with rigidity. The stiff-person syndrome bears the closest similarity to the patient presented here. ... our patient had anti-GAD antibodies in serum (109 U/mL; radioimmunoassay) and oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid that, even if not pathognomonic, are widely reported in stiff-person syndrome.

extractions.quote: Needle electromyography (EMG) was performed in the brachial biceps, first dorsal interosseous, quadriceps, and tibialis anterior muscles on the right side. The analysis of motor unit potentials demonstrated polyphasic and large motor unit potentials. A decreased recruitment was also found. Routine nerve conduction studies were performed in ulnar, peroneal, and sural nerves on the right side. ... Surface EMG recordings were obtained using bipolar silver chloride electrodes placed 2 to 4 cm apart longitudinally over the muscle bellies. We recorded from the quadriceps, biceps femoris, tibialis anterior, triceps surae, thoracolumbar, and cervical paraspinal muscles on both sides. The results were confirmed by needle EMG. ... Cutaneomuscular/exteroceptive reflexes were elicited after a single shock delivered to the tibial nerve at the ankle according to the technique described by Meinck et al. ... Somatosensory evoked potentials and motor evoked potentials did not detect any sign of long tract involvement. ... the spasms could be induced by electrical shocks delivered at the ankle or by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the motor cortex.

Cutaneomuscular/exteroceptive reflexes were of an abnormally low threshold. Stimulus at three times the sensory threshold gave consistent short and long latency responses in tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, vastus lateralis, biceps femoris (Fig. 1).
